recovered_records.title: A lightweight CNN supported by partially skip-connected CAE for plant disease identification across multiple agricultural environments
recovered_records.abstract: The increasing global population calls for sustainable agricultural solutions, including automated plant disease identification. Presently, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) require complex architectures and large labeled datasets, relying on transfer learning and data augmentation, particularly in uncontrolled field conditions. Moreover, models trained in controlled environments often surpass those trained in uncontrolled settings due to background variability. To address these challenges, a lightweight CNN architecture supported by the Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE) is proposed capable of operating in both controlled and uncontrolled environments. The CAE model, composed of the encoder and the decoder, optimizes feature extraction with fewer data samples and convolutional layers. The encoder serves as a feature extractor, while an external classification branch uses a fully connected layer with softmax activation to predict class labels. To enhance the reconstruction and feature extraction, a partially skip-connected architecture is added between the encoder and the decoder of the CAE. During training, a combined loss function is integrated to optimize both reconstruction and classification losses, simultaneously. During inference, only the encoder and classification branch are retained, reducing complexity. The system is evaluated across intra-domain, cross-domain, and mixed-domain settings using datasets from various environments. A high accuracy is achieved in controlled conditions (97.05% on PlantVillage, 98% on Citrus, 97.6% on PLD) and demonstrates adaptability in uncontrolled environments (95.14% on Bean, 29.14% on PlantDoc, 81.98% on FieldPlant) without dataset-specific tuning or transfer learning. The full architecture used during training contains approximately 0.72M parameters, while inference requires only 0.30M parameters, making it suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices.

recovered_records.title: Research on beamforming offloading resource allocation based on deep reinforcement learning and ISAC in autonomous vehicle scenarios
recovered_records.abstract: Under the development of 5G-A/6G and intelligent transportation, jointly designing integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) and mobile edge computing (MEC) is important for efficient vehicular edge computing (VEC). Most existing works treat ISAC design and task offloading separately, which makes it difficult to balance sensing reliability and computation latency in dynamic vehicular scenarios. This paper considers a full-duplex ISAC–VEC system with uplink–downlink coupling and formulates a delay minimization problem under a sensing SNR constraint. The receive beamformers are derived using generalized Rayleigh quotient structures, and the remaining resource and offloading decisions are optimized via an RQ-assisted deep deterministic policy gradient (RQ-DDPG) algorithm to improve learning stability in our setting. Simulation results show that the proposed approach achieves lower task latency while maintaining the required sensing performance compared with the considered benchmark schemes.

recovered_records.title: A comparative study of optimization algorithms in physics-informed neural networks for singularly perturbed differential equations
recovered_records.abstract: Differential Equations (DEs) are a versatile mathematical tool for tackling a myriad of real-world challenges. The resolution of such differential problems aids in the advancement of our human environment, prompting the exploration of various techniques and methods for solving these equations. This paper presents a new method employing deep learning principles to tackle differential equations, with a specific focus on real-world issues commonly modelled by Singularly Perturbed Differential Equations (SPDEs), such as those found in fluid mechanics and biosciences. Our approach involves solving these specific problems using neural networks, and employing feed-forward frameworks for their resolution. This paper not only focuses on solving the differential equations but also delves into the optimization process. In particular, we utilized the gradient descent algorithm as our optimizer, exploring five variants of this algorithm. Consequently, we investigate the considered SPDEs using a standard Physics-Informed Neural Network framework combined with five different gradient-based optimization algorithms and evaluated through five performance metrics. The numerical results demonstrate that certain optimization strategies exhibit superior accuracy, convergence behavior, and robustness in approximating the solutions of SPDEs. These findings suggest that the proposed comparative methodology provides useful guidance for selecting optimization algorithms and can be extended to a broad class of differential equations.

recovered_records.title: Physics-informed learning for collective behavior prediction
recovered_records.abstract: Collective behaviors, such as those observed in bird flocks and fish schools, exhibit highly coordinated, self-organized motion. Predicting their trajectories is crucial for understanding collective intelligence and guiding unmanned systems. Existing methods face limitations, as traditional mechanism models rely on oversimplified assumptions and generalize poorly, while purely data-driven models lack interpretability and struggle to adapt to unseen behaviors. Here, we propose a physics-informed decomposition linear neural network (PI-DLinear). By treating the physical parameters in the classic Cucker-Smale model as learnable variables, our framework implements a dynamic physics-constraining module that adapts to underlying interaction mechanisms across diverse collective behaviors. Evaluated on multiple real-world biological datasets (including jackdaw and fish), PI-DLinear significantly improves prediction accuracy within each collective behavior and consistently enhances zero-shot cross-behavior transfer relative to the architecture-matched DLinear baseline, while also demonstrating robustness in small-sample and noisy conditions. By integrating interpretable physical equations with neural networks, our work establishes a paradigm for trajectory prediction that combines interpretability with data-driven flexibility, with promising applications in biological behavior analysis and multi-agent cooperative control.

recovered_records.title: Neural surrogate–driven constrained binary optimization for sensor placement in anomaly detection for hydrogen transport networks
recovered_records.abstract: In recent years, the increasing adoption of distributed sensing systems and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies has enabled denser monitoring infrastructures in industrial and safety-critical environments. In this context, sensor placement in hydrogen transport networks represents a combinatorial optimization problem that affects the information available for anomaly monitoring while being subject to deployment constraints. To address this problem, we propose a formulation based on Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO), in which the energy function is constructed from changes in the reconstruction loss of a neural autoencoder. These changes are measured when individual pressure sensors or sensor pairs are added to a fixed set of mass-flow sensors. Individual and pairwise terms encode measured sensor effects in the quadratic objective. The number of selected sensors is controlled through an energy penalty that discourages configurations whose cardinality deviates from a predefined target, rather than through a hard constraint. The resulting QUBO is mapped to the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) using a variational quantum circuit with alternating cost and mixer layers. Its parameters are optimized through evolutionary search followed by local refinement via a memetic strategy. The experimental analysis compares this approach with classical and exact methods on the same QUBO and examines how faithfully the pairwise objective represents larger sensor configurations and downstream anomaly-detection outcomes. At a target of five pressure sensors, QAOA returned cardinality-feasible configurations in 7/25, 16/25, and 14/25 runs for Gestdown, Gestcenter, and Gestup, respectively, compared with 25/25 runs for each classical baseline in all three topologies.

recovered_records.title: Physics-informed multi-sensor fusion framework for predicting weld penetration state and mechanistic discovery in CMT welding
recovered_records.abstract: Accurate recognition of weld states is essential for ensuring structural integrity in cold metal transfer (CMT) welding. However, it remains challenging to develop models that are both robust to industrial disturbances and physically interpretable. In addition, the inherent opacity of current data-driven methods often limits their reliability in complex manufacturing environments. This study proposes ASPIS-Net, a robust physics-informed network for interpretable CMT weld-state monitoring. The proposed network adopts a dual-branch architecture with an adaptive gated fusion mechanism, which dynamically suppresses environmental noise while preserving critical acoustic and electrical features. To improve model transparency, a symbolic regression framework is further introduced to convert the learned representations into explicit physical equations, thereby aligning deep-learning predictions with the underlying welding thermodynamics. The proposed method was validated using an automated CMT welding platform, from which 5,000 synchronised acoustic and electrical signal samples were collected under four typical penetration states. The results show that ASPIS-Net achieves a classification accuracy of 99.36% and retains a Macro-F1 score of 75.59% under the 0 dB composite-noise condition. This work provides a transparent, physics-guided approach for monitoring multi-physics manufacturing processes, establishing a rational basis for assessing structural reliability in critical welded joints.

Global sensitivity analysis shows that drug elimination and stem-cell parameters govern treatment outcome. We train a physics-informed neural network as a one-step propagator with a structure-preserving increment bound (held-out ) and use it as the environment of a deep reinforcement learning agent. At nominal parameters the learned closed-loop policy (median objective over five seeds) is comparable to an optimised open-loop schedule ( ) and better than a tuned Pontryagin schedule ( ). With error in all parameters it eradicates the model tumour in of cases, against and , by adapting the total dose to the parameters that govern outcome, at the cost of more toxicity events ( against at most ). recovered_records.title: Emergent parallels between language models and the brain.
recovered_records.abstract: How does the brain give rise to human capabilities like language processing or logical reasoning? This question has captured the minds of many cognitive scientists and neuroscientists, and indeed has a history dating back at least as far as the philosophers of ancient Greece. Until recently, humans were the only systems that we knew of that showed these capacities across broad domains. But after recent developments in the field of artificial intelligence, language models have begun to show some surprising parallels to complex cognitive capacities and the neural representations that underpin them - despite the architectures and learning paradigms of these models differing dramatically from biological systems. In this primer, I will provide a brief overview of language models, their construction and training, and the phenomena of natural intelligence that they might help us to understand. First, let us begin with a bit of history.
